definition: Emollient means having a softening, calming effect on something hard, rough, or inflamed.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word emollient. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know emollient should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The ambassador's emollient answers at the border talks cooled a week of angry headlines.
Mild merely refrains from irritating — mild soap does no harm, but it stops well short of emollient's active softening.
Soothing eases the sting, yet it stops short of emollient, which goes on to soften what was cracked, hardened, or tense.

Softening is the plainest name for the work an emollient does: making something hard or stiff pliable again. But softening names only the action, while emollient describes the character of whatever performs it — the cream, the tone, the diplomatic answer that leaves hardness workable.

Comforting eases distress and makes someone feel safe — a comforting word after bad news. Emollient works on hardness rather than sadness: it takes something rough, cracked, or tense and leaves it supple again, whether that is chapped skin or a stalled negotiation.

Emollient names anything that soothes and softens — literally, like a balm on rough skin, or figuratively, like the calm words that soften a tense meeting.
Where 'soothing' only calms, emollient goes a step further: it leaves what was hard or cracked workable again.
Emollient is at home on a pharmacy label and in diplomatic reporting alike — anything, cream or sentence, that softens what it touches.
If you only mean 'calming,' soothing is plainer; reach for emollient when hardness is being worked soft.
Its cousin mollify, which you met earlier in this course, does the same work as a verb: you mollify an angry person, and an emollient tone is how.

The orchard crew dreaded February, when wind and cold split the skin along their knuckles.
The foreman's grandmother had left him a recipe -- beeswax, lanolin, a little olive oil -- and a tin of it lived in every truck.
The balm was genuinely emollient: it did not just coat the cracks or dull the sting, it worked the hardened skin soft again, so hands could close around a pruning saw by morning.
A sales rep once offered the crew a cheaper lotion that promised only to be gentle.
The foreman handed it back; in his orchard, he said, gentle was not the job -- the job was undoing what the wind had done.
